I have some schooling, so I can read the words on a seed packet and I have been to a few cooperative meetings, but I still farm the way my mother taught me and I watch what my neighbors do. My bean plot is only 0.33 hectares, and every kwacha matters to me — I cannot spend money on a full bag of chemical fertilizer for such a small piece of land, and besides, beans do not need it the way maize does. I will spread manure and compost that I have collected around the homestead, because it costs me nothing and I own this land so I want to keep the soil in good heart. I will plant the bean seed I saved from last season — I know it grows well here, and I am not going to risk precious cash on new seed from the agro-dealer when I am not sure it will do better. I will not buy any pesticides or herbicides; my family and I will pull the weeds by hand and pick off any insects we see. We have no irrigation here, so we wait for the rains like we always do. My family will work this plot ourselves for about twenty days from the time we prepare the land until we finish harvesting, and I will not hire any outside labor because I do not have the money to pay wages.
